title: scatter-gather-serialization-latency-investigation
content:
Quick summary:
- We observed intermittent 99th percentile inference latency spikes when serving small, fragmented tensors across replicas during multi-shard requests. Root cause appears to be CPU-side serialization/packing + small-message inefficiencies on the interconnect rather than pure NCCL algorithmic scaling.

Hypothesis we chased:
- When tensors are split into many sub-chunks for shard-aware dispatch, host CPU spends nontrivial cycles serializing metadata+payload, leading to queuing on PCIe/NVLink and causing NCCL to see bursty small messages.
- NCCL handles large contiguous buffers well, but its micro-paths for many small, back-to-back sends amplify latency tails.

Testbed + config:
- Cluster: 4-node test, each node dual-80GB-A100, NVLink pairs fully enabled; IB EDR 100Gbps between nodes.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime/branch perf/async-agg-v2, CUDA 12.1, NCCL 2.20.5, grpc disabled for intra-node.
- Workload: 2.7B encoder-only model sharded with tensor-parallelism=4, pipeline-parallelism=1. Synthetic infer trace replay using real user prompt mix (avg request size ~220 tokens).
- Measurement tools: perf, nvprof/NSys, tracepoints for host serialization, eBPF to measure syscalls and memcpy hotspots, ibstat counters, custom microbench for small-message NCCL timings.

Observations:
- Host serialization time per request measured at 0.6-1.1ms median, 3.5-7.8ms p99 for small-shard cases. This includes packing header, slicing tensors, and staging into pinned buffers.
- PCIe backpressure periods correlate with host side memcpy spikes; when several replicas start concurrently we saw queues form in host staging thread.
- NCCL small-message latency path exhibited skew: instead of steady 30-60us for larger messages, 256-2KB slices were 200-800us and showed higher variance.
- Inter-node runs worse than intra-node: IB latency and QP churn added 30-50% to p99.
- Enabling GPUDirect RDMA cut p99 host CPU by ~30% and reduced end-to-end p99 by ~18% in the inter-node case.

Micro-experiments and results:
1) Coalesce-before-send: aggregated multiple small slices into a single buffer before NCCL call. Result: throughput steady, p99 down 35%, median unchanged. Tradeoff: adds a few hundred microseconds serialization to each request but prevents many micro-NCCL ops.
2) Double-buffering + async memcpy: overlap host pack with previous chunk transfer. Result: decreases median host time by 40% and p99 by 22%. Complexity increases and requires careful pinned buffer pool sizing.
3) Message-size threshold routing: for messages <1KB, route via a different path that batches across requests for short windows (2-4ms). Result: improved p99 but introduced occasional additional latency for individual requests that missed the batch window.
4) NCCL tuning: tried NCCL_P2P_DISABLE, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME tweaks, and ring vs tree algorithms. No free lunch; selecting tree reduced variance for small messages but cost throughput for large transfers.

Profiling artifacts:
- Flamegraphs attached in Confluence link show host pack thread dominated by memcpy and header formatting; syscalls mainly futex for lock contention on buffer pool.
- eBPF shows ~12-28% CPU overhead attributable to buffer zeroing and per-slice memcpy.
- NSight traces indicate NVLink utilization is bursty with many small spikes instead of a smooth utilization curve.

Mitigations proposed (short-term):
- Implement coalescing layer inside serving runtime: opportunistically aggregate contiguous slices belonging to the same global request into one NCCL op. Configurable coalesce threshold with percentile-driven defaults.
- Replace naive memcpy with vectorized packing (SIMD memops) and reuse pinned buffers to avoid zeroing. Add per-thread buffer caches to reduce lock contention.
- Expose a runtime flag to enable GPUDirect RDMA for customers with IB capable networks; add validation checks at startup.

Longer-term ideas:
- Adaptive small-message strategy: runtime keeps a running distribution of slice sizes and dynamically switches between coalescing, batching, or direct sends to minimize tail latency for the active workload.
- Investigate hybrid gather that uses light-weight on-GPU rendezvous for tiny metadata (offsets) and pushes payload via fewer bulk transfers.
- Work with NCCL upstream to optimize small-message kernels or expose a fast path for aggregations. Share benchmarks and telemetry.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do these mitigations interact with KV cache prefetch in real traffic? Could coalescing harm cache-hit latency?
- Pacing: should the runtime intentionally throttle request dispatch to smooth NVLink utilization instead of maximizing parallelism? Need an A/B test across production traffic.
- PCIe vs NVLink tradeoffs on mixed vendor topologies. We only tested homogeneous A100 nodes; need Ampere->Hopper mixed tests.

Action items / next steps:
- Ayesha to PR a coalescing prototype and perf tests (target: PR by end of sprint). Link: GH PR placeholder in linked_artifacts.
- Marcus to run mixed-node (A100+H100) microbench suite and report differences (due 2026-03-20).
- Elena to instrument production canary with lightweight sampling for slice-size distribution and p99 spikes (Confluence dashboard card).
- Samir to draft an addition to the runtimes perf guide describing buffer-pool tuning and pinned memory sizing.

Notes to self / shorthand:
- prioritize p99 over median for customer impact; coalescing seems highest-win with low rollout risk.
- watch out for increased latency variance when batching across requests.

Attachments and traces live in Confluence and GH artifacts listed above.
